slides.heading: Same Bsts
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Hard · Binary Search Trees
slides.narration: Let's solve Same Bsts, a hard binary search trees problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: Would inserting the two arrays (left to right) produce identical BSTs, without building them?
Recurse on first-smaller / first-greater-or-equal descendants within value bounds, using indices only.
slides.narration: Here's the problem. Would inserting the two arrays (left to right) produce identical BSTs, without building them? Recurse on first-smaller / first-greater-or-equal descendants within value bounds, using indices only.

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: Two arrays give the same BST if they share the root and their smaller and larger elements build the same subtrees.
slides.narration: Two arrays give the same BST if they share the root and their smaller and larger elements build the same subtrees.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: Build both BSTs and compare → O(n²) worst
Split into smaller/larger lists recursively → O(n²) time and space
Index-based recursion with bounds → O(n²) time, O(d) space
slides.narration: Building both trees and comparing is straightforward. Without building, we can recursively compare roots and split each array into smaller and larger values. Passing indices and bounds avoids copying.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 2. Split each into smaller and bigger-or-equal lists keeping order
slides.narration: Step by step. First, compare first elements and lengths. Second, split each into smaller and bigger-or-equal lists keeping order. Third, recurse on both halves.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Same root? 10 = 10 ✓
slides.narration: Both arrays start with ten, so the roots match.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Left subtrees: [8, 5, 2] vs [8, 5, 2]
slides.narration: Values smaller than ten, in order, form the left subtree. Both start with eight; recurse.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Right subtrees: first is 15 in both
slides.narration: Values at least ten form the right subtree. Both begin with fifteen. Recursing all the way, everything matches.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Same BST
slides.narration: So both arrays build exactly this BST, without us ever building it.

slides.heading: Java solution (1/2)
slides.narration: Same compares the current roots, then recurses on the first smaller element in range and the first bigger element in range, for both arrays, narrowing the min and max bounds.

slides.heading: Java solution (2/2)
slides.narration: Same compares the current roots, then recurses on the first smaller element in range and the first bigger element in range, for both arrays, narrowing the min and max bounds.

slides.heading: Complexity
slides.narration: Time is O of n squared. Space is O of d.

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
slides.narration: Duplicates go to the right subtree. Different lengths mean different trees.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: Two arrays give the same BST if they share the root and their smaller and larger elements build the same subtrees.
